subject: biology
title: Sex Chromosomes & X-Linked Traits
welcome_lead: Today you'll see why boys are more likely to be colour-blind — by mastering the XX/XY system and how dad decides the baby's sex.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology sex inheritance — XX vs XY, sex-linked traits (colour blindness, haemophilia), probability crosses.
final_note: You learned that dad's sperm decides the baby's sex, why X-linked recessive conditions hit boys more, and how to calculate sex-linked cross probabilities.

concepts.def: Any chromosome that is NOT a sex chromosome
Trait carried on the X chromosome
Female (Xᴬ Xᵃ) who has the allele but isn't affected

walkthroughs.body_html:
Females are XX. Males are XY.

Mum's eggs always carry an X. Dad's sperm carry X or Y.

So dad's sperm decides the baby's sex — and it's a 50/50 split.

Some genes sit only on the X chromosome — colour blindness and haemophilia are classic examples.

Boys (XY) have only one X. One bad allele = condition shows.

Girls (XX) need two bad alleles. With just one, they're a carrier.

Carrier mum (Xᴬ Xᵃ) × normal dad (Xᴬ Y).

Daughters: half Xᴬ Xᴬ (normal), half Xᴬ Xᵃ (carriers). None affected.

Sons: half Xᴬ Y (normal), half Xᵃ Y (affected). So 50% of sons are colour-blind.

mcqs.q: Which parent's gamete determines the sex of the baby?
options: Mum's egg
Dad's sperm
Both equally
Neither — it's random after fertilisation

mcqs.q: Why are boys more likely than girls to be colour-blind?
options: They have stronger genes
Boys only have one X chromosome, so one recessive allele is enough
The Y chromosome causes colour blindness
Girls cannot be colour-blind

mcqs.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed — there's no second X to mask it.
X-linked recessive conditions affect more males because the Y chromosome makes the disease worse.
X-linked conditions affect only males because females cannot inherit X-linked alleles.

mcqs.q: What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
X-linked conditions affect only males because females cannot inherit X-linked alleles.
A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
